body: The course will 'officially' start towards the end of October 2026 and run until the exam in January 2027 (Approx 3 months) I will upload a schedule here closer to the time
If you're going through this before the end of October 2026:

The free preview will be enough to get you started. The intro's are helpful to start understanding the type of study shifts I want you to consider, and obviously decide whether this is right for you. There will be a live session in mid-October. The link will be in the free preview, (Scroll to S2, you'll find all the live sessions and recordings as the course continues) so you can join regardless of whether you've registered and paid. (If you're registered on the course, I'll email you with the date when it's finalised.
If you do register for the full course, you can start the Tasks once you've worked through the Intro sections.
Live Sessions will be on Tuesdays evenings at 18:00 SAST, generally every second week, unless we need more of them.

My diary will be open for your one-on-ones as soon as you register. The sooner you book, the better. It's better to have this session as you start the course (unless you've worked with me before and feel you don't need this). The evening sessions are always booked quickly, so get in there ASAP (Even if it means booking a month in advance).
(I will upload a study schedule indicating the live session dates and approximate Task completion dates before the end of October)

While I provide dates and deadlines to try keep everyone on track, the course is on-demand, which means you do the Tasks at your own pace. If you start earlier, you have more time to work on your Skills. If you start later, you'll need to do the Tasks a little faster to make sure you have enough time for completion and to make the Skills your own.
Some students work through the Tasks really quickly to get through the work and focus on the application of these in their exam prep - This is great.
How long will it take you to work through the course?
I want you to have at LEAST two weeks before the exam where you apply and integrate the Skills you've learnt and use them to improve your final prep and questions.

There are at 6 compulsory tasks and a sim exam. Most students do a task a week, if they've started in November. If you start later than that, you need to do more. Each task will take about two hours to work through the Skill videos and methods, and then two hours to do the question and submit it to me. On average, you're looking at seven weeks of this course.
When should you plan to finish the course?

You HAVE to have time after the course is complete to make sure that you're using the Skills we've covered. If you've done something once, it isn't 'yours', and when you get into the exam, you're going to go straight back to your old habits under that stress. You have to make these Skills 'normal' - and that means practicing AFTER the course is over. Do NOT schedule your time to finish my sim exam the week of the exam, there's not much advice I can give you to help you improve what you're doing.
What if you finish 'early'?

You're still on the course, still attending the live sessions, and most students email me to discuss Skills they're working on and how it's going, getting advice etc. So, you may be finished the official Tasks... but you're never alone

body: We'll help you USE the knowledge you already have, so you get marks for what you do know
You can improve your revision by focussing on areas and skills you're not able to use
We know you still have revision you want to do, but we want you to practice getting those marks

Each Task builds on the previous one, and you can't move to the next one without submitting the previous one. You're layering your Skills as you go.
Our feedback focusses on your Skills. We're aware you're still working on some of your revision.
After you've completed the Skills, combine your new super-powers and attempt a full Sim Exam (Past ITC paper). Mark and submit to us for individual feedback.
Our focus is on how you're applying the Skills we've covered.

lessons.title: L4 - Lecturer Feedback and Help
body: I KNOW that you still have revision to do. I KNOW that you're going to fail the questions you attempt. My advice remains the same. Focus on questions. I am here to support you through this.

Each of the tasks you submit will get feedback from me. I will look at your case study, required, the planning you did, your answer, your marking and the study form you complete. From all of this, I get a great idea of what's going through your head as you answer.
I am looking specifically for your application of the SKILL for that task. I'm not particularly interested in your marks, or your knowledge levels. Here's some of the types of feedback you'll get:
You may identify that you need more revision, I may disagree based on what I can see your understanding is, or perhaps I'll agree with you
I may advise that you need a different approach in your thinking
I'll let you know if your marking is inaccurate
I can identify whether your case study planning is useful for your answering
I'll give you advice related to the specific Skill you're currently working on, and how to improve, whether I feel you should redo something
And last but not least, it's really encouraging to see that you're not as far off as you might feel you are.
You have access to all the CTA syllabus content, so you will find the knowledge you need from there.

I am here to help you, but this is not a theory-based course, so I will not be answering technical questions. I will however, help you find the answers and learn for yourself (which is far more important). I will always challenge your thinking and approach before I suggest a theory approach:
Are you trying to circumvent questions and go back to revision? (This is a very powerful and magnetic comfort zone, do NOT underestimate it).
Have you tried ANYTHING relating to this area? Or are you assuming without trying that you 'know nothing'?
Are you avoiding doing a question because you know you'll fail it, and you don't want to fail anything?
I try get your feedback to you within two or three days. The closer we get to exams, the tougher this can be, with the volume of submissions. So, start early!
You don't need to wait for my feedback before you start the next Skill, so I won't hold you back! But don't do more than two tasks before you hear from me.

I'm here to help you, so talk to me. Whether things are going well or badly, I'm here for you. When things are bad, that's when you need the support the most. Don't go quiet when you're struggling with something.
I'll put in as much effort and engagement as you do, and then some. I am committed to your success, as long as you are.

body: You can find the link to this on SAICA's website
Look for B and Ba (Appendix 1 - An excel file)

'Enabling competencies' are increasing in focus for IAC. In the past, ONLY 'communication' marks were awarded. Thus, the only Enabling Competency' that was awarded separate marks for was communication. These have now been expanded to quite a few items in the Enabling Competencies categories.
This doesn't require 'new' studying, it requires an awareness of the continued shift to assessing your underlying skills
This is SAICA's 'list' of the stuff you need to know for your IAC exam. There are three main components:
Professional Values & Attitudes (PVAA)
Enabling Competencies ('acumens')
Technical Competencies (Your subject knowledge)

Each of these have a bunch of categories within them, and represent the stuff that can be examined and how. (Most of your subject-matter will be under the Technical Competencies, so that one you'll be more familiar with).
The PVAA consist of the 'values and attitudes' of the following (pg14) and are all broken down further as well:
Ethics (Personal, Business, Professional)
Citizenship (Personal, Corporate)
Lifelong learning (Self development, Adaptive mindset & agility; Emotional Intelligence)
Enabling Competencies are also broken down (pg22):
Relational Acumen (Communication skills are in here)

body: I am absolutely behind you :) I have a ton of feedback to do, obviously as we get closer to the exam I get flooded with more tasks and sim exams. So I need to focus my time on getting people their feedback, this means I can’t be answering individual emails as much, and most of the emails at this point are the same… “How do I study from now on…?”… and my advice is mostly the same. So…
Before you send me an email asking me how YOU should study, please read the following :)
Basic assumptions for EVERYONE (ie: if this is you, the same advice below STILL applies)
You’re still failing questions
There’s a ton of theory you don’t know
You feel stupid, possibly more stupid than you usually do this close to the exam
You don’t feel like you’re making enough progress considering how close that exam is getting
There are entire topics you feel like you can’t remember
You feel like you haven’t done ‘enough’ up to now because you’ve been working and haven’t had as much study leave as you wanted
There’s just not enough time to fit it all in.
Now… whichever applies to you:
If you haven’t finished the tasks

Finish the tasks. The point of these is to provide you with tools to use to get a few extra marks for ANY question you do. I realise that you’re quietly (or not-so-quietly!) freaking out about all the theory and topics you haven’t touched. But if you can’t get marks for what you already know… you need to work on the skill of getting marks there before you go gathering more stuff that you still won’t get marks for.

Make notes of the stuff you want to do more ‘revision’ for later and get on with the tasks. The sooner you get them done, the sooner you can work on questions and improve all your stuff, including your theory.

Do the sim exam as soon as you’re done with the tasks. The sim exam is there to help you practice applying the skills you’ve just done. I don’t care if you fail. It’s NOT there to assess whether you’re going to pass, so don’t ‘save’ it for later when you feel you’ll be ‘better’ at stuff.

You’re going to fail it. Deal with it. The purpose is to start working on improving and consolidating those skills you’ve just finished, so that you can approach ALL the rest of your studying with better skills.
If you’ve finished the tasks and sim exam
I have a video about how to approach the rest of your studies: https://courses.accountingstudyadvice.com/courses/take/iac-skills-course-june-2025/texts/63924126-l5-full-sim-exams-or-smaller-questions

This is to discuss how to balance out all the ‘stuff’ you want to do - Short questions, topic-based questions, sim-exams (long questions), and blind questions. Please watch this before you email me and ask what YOU should do. I’m going to refer you back to this video.

In the video, I advise doing 3 or 4 days of short questions, then a full exam. This is more sustainable than thinking you’re some kinda of super-human who’s going to be able to do and mark full sim exams every day from now until the exam. We know how that ends - you do this for three days, then fall apart and do nothing for another three days.. or you go back to theory because you’re exhausted and can’t face another question with the MASSIVE list of stuff that you’ve realised you don’t know.

Do the full sim, (and include SAICA’s mock exams in this) and use the short questions after that to close the gaps you’ve identified. In the sim feedback, I might give you some advice on stuff you should focus on or redo… that will be something you can work into your studying, but I’m not going to give you any kind of ‘different’ advice that totally changes what I’m advising above. So, don’t send me an email for ‘specific’ advice and then ‘wait’ for me to tell you how to study this weekend. I may not be able to get back to you fast enough for you to be productive.
General advice for everyone (and answers to a lot of questions I get):

Doing questions IS REVISION We somehow see questions and revision as two totally separate things.. I get it, but it’s NOT. You KNOW that you end up doing revision when you’re marking. You ALWAYS go back to ‘check’ the sections or theory when you’re marking and wondering where in the sections / theory that point comes from. And you ‘refresh’ your theory when you’re marking and thinking “AH yeah, I forgot about that one, and how it applies to xxx situation”. - THIS IS REVISION. It may not be the ENTIRE amount of revision you want to do for that topic, but it’s incredibly valuable revision.

Doing revision through questions Do the question, mark the question, and leave ONE HOUR to do the ‘fix’. Pick one or two things to work on. If you had to write an exam on that topic in an hour, what ‘revision’ would you work on in that hour? This type of revision is incredibly valuable because you’re working on the theory in the context of how to USE it in situations, as opposed to the ‘flat’ theory of “The section says xxx”… yeah, but HOW do you use it? How do you identify when to use it? How do you apply it to different situations? THIS is where the marks come from.

Exhausting days… consistency is more important than small bursts of insane energy and then nothing Yeah, doing questions all day is insanely exhausting. And it feels like you can never do enough. We need to make sure you can actually keep going consistently until that exam. We generally make the mistake of approaching this like a sprint, especially if we’ve just gone on study leave. We plan to do ALL the stuff we’ve been putting off because we were still working (Sound familiar?! Lol). We go at it like a rabid monkey… for about three days… then we fall over. Do three short questions a day. Stick to one subject. Do the questions when you’re fresher, the morning / day generally. And then do two or three hours of your ‘revision’ at night. The revision is always a little less exhausting than the question, so save that for after supper. Your questions are still fresh in your mind, so it’s valuable, and you can be a little less drained. Three questions a day IS possible, if you stop the procrastination, the pre-question revision, the ‘hunting’ for and ‘saving’ of questions, and all the other ‘stuff’ we end up doing ‘around’ the studying because we just struggle with the ‘sit down and DO it’ part ;) Totally understandable. If you do this for four days, you’ll have done 12 questions and 12 hours of theory. So, while you feel like there’s never enough you can do… that approach is very effective and gets a lot done.

lessons.title: What will we cover in Task 1?
body: "I'm not ready to do questions! I still have to do revision!"

Is this you?! Course it is! Most students feel this way. Whether you did PGDA a while back, failed ITC, or just have that feeling that you're not on top of your game and need to revise before you get to questions... you cannot get away from that feeling that you have quite a bit of work to do BEFORE you touch questions.
How do you KNOW when you have ENOUGH theory to pass questions?

Wouldn't it be awesome to be able to calculate this? To really KNOW whether you know enough to pass Introducing... the BMCR, your new BFF! This is a marking tool designed to help you identify what you need to focus on. Do you really need to study more theory? Do you need to work on application? Communication?

The BMCR is going to show you just how much you know, and whether you're getting marks for ANYTHING you know. We're going to give you a specific methodology for marking your questions, and assessing and analysing your BMCR. (BMCR: 'Basic Mark Conversion Ratio')
We HATE the feeling of 'not knowing' the answer
The BMCR will PROVE whether you need theory or not. But that won't change the FEELING that you have that you need to still do theory.
We're going to help you 'change your mind!'

We can't 'just change' the way we feel and think, we need to MAKE a change, and that means taking control of the way we think and actively changing our thought processes. We're going to give you a specific tool to 'change your mind'. I call it 'Reframing'. I love it! You will too.

lessons.title: "Why don't I do questions!? What's wrong with me!?"
body: I'm willing to bet that when Task 1 popped up, with the IMMEDIATE requirement of DOING A QUESTION, you started looking for a way out, an escape route of some sort.

You resist doing questions. You don't do them until you're 'ready'. Yet you KNOW how important they are, you KNOW you need to do them, even though you don't know all your stuff... so WHY is it so tough?

There are a few concepts I'll explain in this section for you that will CHANGE YOUR LIFE (That's a promise!) if you take a few minutes to think about it, and will help you understand why you study the way that you do.
'The Chair' is what I use to refer to the feelings of discomfort we have when we're in situations where we don't know what's going on. Exams, tough questions, classes for topics we don't understand.
These two videos explain the challenge and how it affects us:
How we THINK The Chair works.
The good news? You already have the tool to start changing this: Reframing
Mindset can very simply be described as how you respond when things don't work out. (Massive oversimplification!)
Some people feel that they just need to try again, try something different, get help, keep going... and they'll get there. No stress. No anxiety. It's just part of the journey (Growth'ers)

Some people feel that the obstacle MEANS that they'll never be able to do it. They're not smart enough, nothing will ever change, they'll never get there. Very stressful, highly anxious, and terrified that at some point, they'll get to the end of their 'smartness' and won't be able to go further (Fixed'ers)
Check out these videos to understand this:
What is mindset and how does it affect your studying?
Where does our mindset come from?
Most of us don't have resilience

We KNOW we should do questions, and now we know a bunch of stuff about our mindset and why we're uncomfortable, but we're not aware that there's a really good reason that we don't do questions until we 'feel ready'... BECAUSE WE'VE BEEN TOLD NOT TO!

lessons.title: "How do I learn instead of memorise?"
body: You've heard this a lot, I'm sure. You need to understand your work, be able to apply it and think about it etc. But if we're very used to relying on memory, for theory and for questions and solutions, then HOW do we change this?

In earlier levels of studying, many of us did previous exam papers with some expectation that the exam would have similar questions. Similar enough that you could somewhat 'copy and paste' the solutions from past questions into this one.

At higher levels, this approach no longer works. Every question needs to be solved from scratch, and no past solution fits nicely into it. We can't just 'match' past solutions to the next problem. It doesn't fit! (And I bet you've experienced that already!)
Problem Matching vs Problem Solving

The Chair is important to remember here. We are NOT comfortable in situations where we need to work with a blank page and we don't have SOME form of starting point or structure to use. We NEED some idea of what the solution should look like
Yeah, this may sound a little strange, so check out the video!
Studying is like a screwdriver

This is great learning advice, and it doesn't take long either. You already HAVE a lot of knowledge, but your biggest challenge is that it's not quite 'at home' in your head. It's more like 'flat theory'. Here's some great advice on how to change this:
How to learn stuff properly

In the above video, I talk about getting help if you can't answer some of those questions yourself. If you don't have a lecturer, that can be tricky. But that's not a problem, because now you have ChatGPT! So, let's help you use ChatGPT!

lessons.title: Using ChatGPT as a tutor / lecturer / study guide
body: ChatGPT is a firm favourite of mine. Even on the free version, you can get great help, so let's see how you can get the most of out to hep you study.
I use it a LOT for my own studying, and it's helped me with my understanding and application of knowledge, and SO much faster than a textbook, Google, or waiting for a response for a lecturer.

When most people talk about AI and studying, they focus on the 'cheating' component. Using it to do your work, assignments etc for you. That's not what I'm referring to. There's no learning involved in this, and obviously not helpful for your exams. So, what DO I mean?
In the videos below, I give an example of using ChatGPT to help your understanding of a topic
Using ChatGPT to help with Costing (FinMan)
This tool is really valuable to help you with the skill of 'learning' instead of 'memorising'

In the example video above, I focus on getting it to explain concepts to me. BUT, the best way to learn is to teach, or at the very least, make sure you can express the concepts yourself. So, the most valuable way to use it is to tell it how YOU understand something, and then ask it if you're correct.
Here's an example of a question I asked ChatGPT and how it responded:

Q: I'm auditing with the ISA's. body: You PLAN to study, do questions, stick to your schedule etc, and yet you just DON'T get there. Procrastination, distraction, lack of focus, lack of motivation... WHY do you keep sabotaging yourself when you want this so badly?!

lessons.title: "I don't think I can do this..."
body: A goal like this can challenge the most self-assured person. It's a long road, a lot of sacrifices, years of studying, and it seems never-ending.

Between overwhelm, fear of failure, self-doubt, lack of confidence, lost motivation, complex concepts and exam requirements, we all feel like this may just not be possible at some point. Here's some stuff to think of

This is highly unproductive. (As if we didn't know!) The problem with feeling overwhelmed is that it drops ALL your problems onto your shoulders at once, which mostly has the effect of paralysing you. If stress was positive, and it made you more effective or gave you some aggressive energy to keep going, that would at least be helpful. But overwhelm makes you feel like a deer in the headlights. Let's look at how we can overcome this:

The Brick-a-Day Tool sounds simple, and it is. But it IS effective, and it takes practice. Keep in mind that this tool is not about 'fixing' how much stuff you have to do, it's about changing the way your brain is wired

This feeling can come and go through our studying. We've signed up for this, so there is SOME feeling that we should be able to do it. The problem is when we hit something we can't get around, struggle with for a while, and obviously, failure. One of the first questions we can't help but face is: Perhaps it's because I'm not smart enough. Here's what I want you to know about this:
You ARE smart enough. Don't break my heart.

If you tried to build a house with your hands, you'd fail at it. Not because you can't build houses, but because you need TOOLS. If you didn't know those tools existed, then of COURSE you'll feel useless.

I struggled with confidence in a lot of areas in my life. Studying was DEFINITELY one of them. Like most people, I think I felt that I needed to have that sense of confidence in myself FIRST, and then it would be easier to do 'the hard thing'. I learnt quite a bit about confidence as I explored it for myself and my students. Let me share some of it with you:
What we THINK confidence is
I love that quote, but it is a lot more difficult to FEEL in those moments where we question our intelligence and just can't get something right.

lessons.title: "I struggle with FinMan topics"
body: FinMan topics 'work' differently to our other subjects. Most of the rest of our subjects have 'Rules'. If you know the rules, you can work with the details. With FinMan, there are guidelines, and theory that provide 'Tools' to help us solve problems, but they don't always work the same way, and this can be tricky for us to work with.

Rules need to be studied in a certain way. You need to learn the details and consistently apply the rule everytime you're in that situation. It always works the same way, and even though it may be complex, it's consistent.

Tools are very different. Tools are there to help you solve a problem, and may look different in every situation you use them. You don't HAVE to do it this way, there are other ways to solve the problem. Your job is to identify the most appropriate tool for the job. That's a totally different way of working and learning.

Students often say they struggle with these because they can't 'think outside the box'. That' not the problem. They need more exposure to the tools and how they're used. Ie: they need to do more questions and see how the tools are used, and get their hands dirty. The more, different situations they experience, the easier it becomes to use the tools.

body: Most of our studies in earlier levels was about learning the answers. We believe that the way to solve problems is to be able to 'know' the answer to questions we're asked. We should know enough to have the shape of the solution pop into our head as we're reading the question.
Let's explore this a little, because it adds a LOT of stress to your studying, and it can also mean you're not studying effectively
This may help. Especially the last one. We remember the FEELING of 'knowing the answer'. Those were good days. And we want to get back there.
Do your lecturers know the answers?
I USED to know the answers!
The more that technology is available to your clients (And we saw in an earlier lesson how helpful ChatGPT can be!), the more your clients have access to the SAME knowledge as you.

lessons.title: "I'm panicking... in studies and exams"
body: We can't say "I lost 10 marks due to stress". It's normally because we didn't read the question properly, rushed, lost track of our thoughts, couldn't think of the concepts etc. We generally think: "If I'd known my work better, I wouldn't have made silly mistakes".
In reality, anxiety and panic affect the way our brains work. You need a Tool to help you calm down when you need to.

As more and more research is done on how to manage our stress levels, deal with tricky situations, and get the best from our brain, we keep hearing that mindful breathing is one of the most powerful, and incredibly fast and easy tools to help us with this. It sounds simple. It is. There's a ton of science behind it, and it will help you take control in your studying and exams.
This is a skill that takes some time to practice. You want to practice this multiple times a day, in calm and stressful situations, so you get your brain used to the idea of doing what you tell it.

My advice is to set an alarm on your phone for a few times a day. When the alarm goes off, practice this. It will take less than a minute. When you're studying, set your alarm for every 10 minutes, and practice this every 10 minutes. Get used to continually taking control back during exams.

lessons.title: L9 - Extra Tool: The Power of 'Thing'
body: What if there's a word / phrase in the case study or required that freaks you out?

The video will explain the process, but as a quick overview, the idea is that when we read a sentence / required that has a 'weird' word / phrase in there that we don't know, it affects our understanding of the whole paragraph / required. It would help if we could 'isolate' the impact of the 'weird' word so that we can get an idea of what the rest of the sentence is, the context, and then 'add' the weird word back later.

Research indicates that the two sides of our brain are responsible for different things. We used to think that the left and right sides of our brains were responsible for different things that were quite separate (ie: Left-brains are creative, and right-brains are analytical), but the reality is more connected and interesting.

When we look at how our brain read and makes sense of information, one side of our brain reads each word one-by-one and makes sense of that one word "What is it? Do I know what it is?", and then it passes onto the other side of our brain to make sense of the sentence as a whole. The one side makes sense of the words, the other side makes sense of the context.

The problem is that if the one side can't make sense of the word, it won't pass it onto the other side. It's stuck there. "I don't know this word, so I'm going to keep it on this side until I make sense of it". So, you don't try to make sense of the sentence and the context, because the one side of your brain isn't finished. If we can find a way to let the one side hand over the information, we can try make sense of the context, even if we don't have that one word. That's where this little 'trick' comes from.

Take a look (if you haven't already!) at the following from SAICA's comments on the Jan 2020 ITC paper: (For this task, I'm focussing on the markers comments on communication)

More that 70% of the last 6 ITC exams have been discussion-type questions. (Describe; Explain; Recommend; Advise; Criticise etc). Students lose a lot of marks here. They KNOW the stuff, but they can't put it in words properly to get the marks.
I'm giving you a basic structure

In educational psychology, this is called 'scaffolding', because I'm giving you structures to help you build skills that you will continue to build on yourself. Kinda like training wheels. We'll just call it stepping stones to improve your discussion questions across all your topics and subjects.
Here are a few challenges we need to work on here:
The balance between theory, application and conclusions
Writing a lot, in a limited amount of time
Adjusting the length of our answers for higher and lower mark allocations
We're not natural 'writers', so it takes us a while to get our thoughts together to make those lovely sentences that are on the solution!

This is going to be game-changing for you. Instead of trying to figure out how you should've known to saw xyz in different questions, you're going to have a more consistent approach to get you marks for what you know.
You need to practice this, but I promise it will improve almost immediately.

lessons.title: L1 - Why do we need to actively work on Communication, even though we know our work?
body: In your head, you can 'see' the answer and information. What we don't realise is that the knowledge and thoughts are like leaves on a tree, they're all over the show. We can see them all at once, but there's no order to them. We also see them in our heads more as pictures or intangible concepts than as words.

When we communicate, we need to put all those thoughts in a specific order, and then articulate them one-by-one, in order. This means we need to pick the 'leaves' off our tree from different places and then put them in order, and then put words to them.

This is also something we're not used to doing. We're generally naturally better at numbers, formats, pattern-recognition and formulae, so this doesn't come naturally to us. It requires practice and deliberate improvement.
Now it makes more sense why we struggle to communicate, even though we know our stuff!

body: "If I know my work better, I'll get better marks"

body: In our FAQ section, I spoke about 'Know vs Build' - The difference between knowing the answer, and building one based on your clients' specific information and situation.
I've also spoken about 'Rules vs Tools' (Quite a bit!).

It takes students a while to realise that the only way that we learn skills is to jump in there and get our hands dirty. We'll fall over, get it wrong, go back a few times, make the same (and different!) mistakes. But the ONLY way we learn is to get started. Expose yourself to different situations so you can see how your knowledge WORKS in different ways and build the skill of application.
There's no way around this. You HAVE to be bad at something in order to get good at it. We seriously struggle with this, so Reframing is incredibly valuable for us.

I've created a worksheet with a list of 'issues' we come across when we do questions. I've set them up as specific questions that you can answer after you've done a question, and using that, we can identify how your application went, and what specific issues you may have struggled with. The skill of 'application' requires a bunch of sub-skills, so the more specific we can be about WHAT the challenge is, the more we can improve.
Let's take a look at a few examples:

When you did the question, did you think of the theory and concept, but you didn't put it in your answer because you didn't trust yourself? You second-guessed yourself and weren't completely sure, so you didn't include it?
This will affect your application (obviously!), but it's not because you 'didn't know' or didn't have the skill. It's a trust issue. The biggest thing you need to work on is:
"If it's in your head, put it on paper"
While you're studying, force yourself to do this, and you can then properly assess whether you can or can't be trusted! And you can learn what you need to improve.
Can you see what I mean? This LOOKS like an application issue, but it's actually a trust and practice issue

When I mark students' questions, I always look at the case study they've planned on. I compare their answer to what they identified in their case study. Often, I can see they identified the issue in the case study, but it doesn't show up in their answer.

So, they know that the information is relevant. That's a good start to application. The question you need to consider for yourself is "Why did you leave it out of the answer?". There may be a few reasons for this, which would require different 'fixes':
Ran out of timeYou need to manage your time better

Again, can you see that this will affect application, but is a completely different issue, and requires a totally different solution to the first example I gave you?

This is REALLY common! Under exam pressure, we THINK we've done something, but when we come back later, we realise we didn't do what we thought. A challenge we have here is that it makes sense in your mind. You see the issue in the case study, you connect it to the theory in your head, and you feel like you've got it sorted. When you write the answer though, you don't realise that you only really focussed on the theory and didn't explicitly connect it to the case study.

This looks like an application issue, because obviously you're not 'applying' your knowledge. In reality, it's more of a communication issue. You can see the application in your mind, but you're not used to, or comfortable with how to communicate it on paper. The more you practice this, and are consciously aware of it, the faster you'll improve.

You answer and application will be inappropriate, but not because you didn't connect the right application to the theory. It's because you thought you were supposed to do 'abc' and that's what you answered. If you'd have read it correctly, you'd be in a better position.
This isn't an application issue, it's a RTFQ issue. You need to work on how you're reading and interpreting the required BEFORE you start answering.

I've given you some specific questions to ask yourself about how the question went. All of these issues are things you can clearly identify and answer, as opposed to a vague comment of "Your application is a problem".
And you can see that although all of these look and smell like application issues, they're actually often different issues.

body: We worked on communication skills in a previous Task. This is a great start, but we also need to know how to evaluate the challenges we have, and obviously how to fix the issues we find. So let's talk about this.
One of the challenges we have here is pretty subtle. The problem is that it makes sense in our head. We can SEE it in our mind.

In your head, you can 'see' the answer and information. What we don't realise is that the knowledge and thoughts are like leaves on a tree, they're all over the show. We can see them all at once, but there's no order to them. We also see them in our heads more as pictures or intangible concepts than as words.

When we communicate, we need to put all those thoughts in a specific order, and then articulate them one-by-one, in order. This means we need to pick the 'leaves' off our tree from different places and then put them in order, and then put words to them.
Now it makes more sense why we struggle to communicate, even though we know our stuff!

This is also something we're not used to doing. We're generally naturally better at numbers, formats, pattern-recognition and formulae, so this doesn't come naturally to us. It requires practice and deliberate improvement.

The more you practice this, and are consciously aware of it, the faster you'll improve.
If your points are taking up five lines or more, you're probably waffling.

The problem here is two-fold. First, you're going to run out of time if you take this long to get to each point. Second, waffling is generally an indication that you're either 'thinking as you write' (ie: you don't really know what you're going to say when you start the sentence, so you're thinking about the sentence as you're writing it), or you're not sure what you're going to say and how to make your point.

Communicating our thoughts and opinions is not something we do in this way very often, so it's natural that we're not great at it. We need to be brief, concise and fast. lessons.title: L5 - How can we fix communication issues?
body: This is part of what we call 'deliberate practice' - which is practicing something with a deliberate outcome. Simply doing more and more discussion questions with the same communication style will take a LONG time to improve, because you're not actively asking yourself what you should change, and actively making those changes.
It may seem annoying, but I promise that it will come right faster than you think!

You may not like the idea, but you know it's got to happen... you're going to have to do some deliberate practice to change the way you structure sentences and be more concise. (Yes, I can hear you groaning from here! But you know I'm right!)
Here's how you're going to fix this:

After you've done a question and marked it, focus on the points in the solution and the way the sentences are structured. You'll often find yourself thinking "Ah, that's a far better way of saying that". If the point is shorter, more concise, clearer, then take a look at how they structured the sentence.

Analyse their approach: What was it they left out? What did they add in that you didn't? How did they state the theory? How did they talk about the info in the case study. (ie: how much of it did they repeat)?

Take a look at the ELEMENTS of the points. For example: In Task 3, we spoke about the 'Is'; 'Should be' and 'So what' (Application, communication, conclusion - Mainly for compliance-type questions). Can you see these elements in their answer? How do they bring it together? Then look at your answer, do you have those elements? Can you spot the application and the conclusion in your point?
It's not necessary to do it for ALL the points, but do a few of them so you start seeing a trend and can see the difference between yours and theirs.

If your communication is really terrible, then redo the question immediately, with the focus on the sentences and trying to copy their style, continuously looking for whether you've included all the elements you wanted to and mark it again, also focussing on the communication. Is there an improvement? Are you getting your points across a little better?

Leave this question for two days, then redo it, focussing on the sentence structure that you preferred. (If your communication needs some improvement, but isn't terrible, then you can skip the previous step of redoing immediately). This is important because two days is just enough for the memory of the sentences to start fading from your brain, but the concepts that you identified are still there. So, you'll remember that you liked something about the sentence, but you won't be able to immediately remember it. That means your brain has to 'work' a little harder to think about it and do it, which strengthens the learning process and skill. When we redo the question straight after doing it, we're mostly rewriting points from memory, as opposed to genuinely changing our communication style. So, leave it for just long enough for the sentence to fade, but the concepts are still there.

Redoing the question when you're working on communication skills is valuable because the second time you do it, your brain is less likely to spend all it's energy on the knowledge issues. You've done the question, you know the answers, you remember a lot of it, so you won't be as focussed on getting the 'answer' right, which allows you to focus on a different skill. Trying this on a new question is trickier because getting your brain to focus on something other than subject-matter is really tough!

lessons.title: Sim Exam 1 - When to do it? Why will this help?
body: Students feel that doing questions, especially sim exams are about identifying whether they 'know their stuff' and whether they're ready to pass yet. This is NOT the purpose of this Sim Exam. So, what is it?

The earlier you do this Sim Exam, the more we can help guide you in terms of what to work on. Knowledge? Application? Communication? Stress? What is costing you marks? Often, it's not what students think, so our feedback is seriously valuable.
Do it ASAP, and let us help guide your studying. You're using the sim exam and feedback to practice your skills, improve your mark gathering, and figure out what else still needs work.

While you're studying, your objective is to LEARN, to IMPROVE, to identify your strengths and weaknesses and work on those, to get FEEDBACK to help you. I want to see your communication style, your structured thinking. So perhaps you identified the wrong theory, I'm still going to look at how you applied, communicated and structured it. This is valuable.
Feedback for students is often 8 or more pages... because I don't tell you "You did this wrong", I tell you "This is HOW TO IMPROVE what you're doing"
You CANNOT find that type of support anywhere else, so take advantage of it!

DIY Tasks - Make the Skills second nature
body: We revert back to the familiar under stress

When we're under stress, we tend to revert back to familiar habits and skills. Your brain can't handle loads of 'new' stuff at once, so if it's faced with a new, stressful case study, then it will probably go back to the exam habits, thinking and communication you've always done.

If you want to make sure you use your new skills in exams, you need to 'make them your own'. Practice them, and get used to using them so that they're not 'new'. When you're under stress, your brain will use these new skills as they're now more familiar.
